newsitem.title: UK: Blair to chair new British cabinet's first meeting.
newsitem.headline: Blair to chair new British cabinet's first meeting.

text.p: British Prime Minister Tony Blair chairs the first meeting of his new Labour cabinet on Thursday to plan a major legislative programme for the next 16 months, saying "we have the chance to do something quite special".

A week after the election which ended 18 years of Conservative rule, Blair's new team will draw up the contents of a speech to be read by Queen Elizabeth when she officially opens parliament next Wednesday.

Blair aides said the speech, traditionally written for the queen by the government, is likely to contain more than a dozen proposals for legislation which the government will push through parliament using its massive 179-seat majority.
"We have the chance to do something quite special, possibly even quite spectacular for the future of our country," he told Labour members of parliament on Wednesday.
The aides said Blair would live up to his election pledge to make education "the passion of my government" by including no fewer than three bills on the subject in the Queen's Speech.
In addition there will be bills on health, law and order, and devolution -- Blair has promised to hold referendums on setting up Scottish and Welsh mini-parliaments by September or October.
The government will also indicate its determination to help the people it claims suffered under the Conservatives.

Blair aides said the Queen's Speech would presage the setting up of a commission to work out proposals for a national minimum wage and would detail its plans to get the unemployed off welfare and into work.

Britain's Channel Four television reported there would also be legislation to ban political parties from accepting funds from foreigners following allegations that overseas businessmen had bankrolled the Conservatives to curry favour with ministers.
The cabinet meeting will be followed by Blair's first talks as Prime Minister with Irish opposite number John Bruton.
But government sources said a new initiative on Northern Ireland could not possibly emerge at the brief encounter at Blair's Downing Street office.
In the week it has been in power, the Blair government has surprised observers with its speed of action.

Finance minister Gordon Brown on Tuesday announced plans to hand control over interest rates to the Bank of England and foreign secretary Robin Cook has rushed to mend fences with Britain's European Union partners.
In a sign he proposes to govern pragmatically, Blair on Wednesday appointed Sir David Simon, chairman of British Petroleum, as minister for trade and competitiveness in Europe.
"He's not a Labour Party member as far as I know," said a spokesman for the prime minister.

The Conservatives, who lost almost half their seats in an election debacle which had historians stumped for precedents, are meanwhile preparing for a possibly bruising leadership battle after John Major's decision to step down.

Six of Major's former cabinet colleagues have now declared they will be candidates to become opposition leader, with the bookmakers making former Welsh Secretary William Hague, at 36 more than seven years younger than Blair, the early favourite.
